strengths: Identifies an important and understudied problem: smoothness errors (oversmoothing and undersmoothing) in GNN dynamics models, and argues convincingly that unitary convolutions can be overconstrained when the target dynamics naturally smooth.
Provides a theoretical lower bound (Theorem 1) on the approximation error of unitary functions via norm variance over SU(n) orbits, giving a principled motivation for relaxing strict unitarity.

Extends the Rayleigh quotient and unitary convolution framework from graphs to meshes using the Robust Laplacian and cotangent weights, with a proof of invariance (Corollary 1). This is a novel and potentially useful generalization for PDEs on manifolds.

Introduces two practical relaxation mechanisms (Taylor truncation and encoder-decoder) and demonstrates that R-UniGraph/R-UniMesh can outperform baselines on heat diffusion, achieving the best NRMSE, SMAPE, and Rayleigh error among mesh PDE tasks for heat.

Empirical study spans grid graphs, complex mesh PDEs, and WeatherBench2 weather forecasting, includes strong baselines (gauge equivariant, Euclidean equivariant, transformer, MPNN), and introduces smoothness metrics (MRE/RE) and qualitative diagnostics.
Reports an anonymous artifact, hyperparameters, and training details, and honestly discusses limitations such as compute constraints, small parameter budgets, and diverging baselines.
weaknesses: The central claim that the paper 'proves unitary convolutions hurt performance' is overstated. Theorem 1 bounds the approximation error of any unitary function when the target norm has angular dependence, but it does not directly show that unitary convolution networks fail, nor is the bound computed on real data to demonstrate it is non-vacuous or tight.

Potential inconsistency in the mesh extension: Definition 3 defines the mesh Rayleigh quotient using the full cotangent weights W (including rewired edges E'), while the unitary mesh convolution uses \tilde{A}=D^{-1/2}(W \odot A)D^{-1/2}. If A is the original mesh adjacency, rewired edges are zeroed and Corollary 1 may not apply to R_M as defined. The paper should clarify whether A is the rewired adjacency.

Equation 4 for the Taylor-relaxed convolution is incomplete and ambiguous: it omits W and X in L^i(X), and Eq. 3 writes exp(A X W) for a non-square matrix, which is not a standard matrix exponential. The intended vectorized operator should be defined explicitly.

The method comparison is limited: Taylor truncation and encoder-decoder relaxations are never compared on the same task, Tmax sensitivity is only studied at initialization, and there is no systematic ablation showing how the degree of relaxation controls the smoothness/accuracy trade-off on the main mesh and weather tasks.

Empirical results are mixed. R-UniMesh is best on heat but not on wave (RE and SMAPE are worse than Transformer/Hermes/EMAN) or Cahn-Hilliard (GemCNN/EMAN/Hermes are better on NRMSE/SMAPE/RE), and WB2 results are below SOTA. Broad claims of outperforming strong baselines or achieving SOTA on diffusive dynamics are not fully supported by the tables.
Table 1 reports only the best run out of 5 for the motivating experiment, which can overstate R-UniGraph's advantage; mean and standard deviation (or median) would give a more reliable comparison.

Baseline comparison fairness is unclear: some baselines are pretrained checkpoints from Park et al. while others are trained by the authors, parameter budgets and convergence criteria differ, and many cells contain dashes without detailed explanation of non-convergence.

Presentation issues reduce clarity: inconsistent naming (e.g., Table 1 caption says R-UNIMESH while the model is R-UniGraph), an incomplete definition of SU(n) in the main text, grammar errors, and insufficient details about mesh rewiring/preprocessing in the experimental setup.

The abstract and introduction overclaim by saying the method 'outperforms several strong baselines, including mesh-aware transformers and equivariant neural networks' and provides 'SOTA performance on diffusive dynamics problems,' whereas the evidence primarily supports a strong advantage on heat diffusion and competitive but not uniformly best performance elsewhere.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and interesting problem: oversmoothing and undersmoothing in GNNs for dynamics modeling, and proposes relaxing strict smoothness preservation via relaxed unitary convolutions.
Extends the Rayleigh quotient and unitary convolution framework from graphs to meshes using cotangent/Robust Laplacian weights, with a proof of Rayleigh quotient preservation under Assumption 1.

Empirical study spans multiple settings: heat diffusion on grid graphs, MeshPDE (heat/wave/Cahn-Hilliard) on PyVista meshes, and WeatherBench2, with a new Rayleigh error metric and qualitative diagnostics.
R-UniMesh shows clear gains on the heat equation on meshes, achieving the best NRMSE, SMAPE, and RE in Table 2 and better matching the true smoothness in Fig. 4.
Includes a sensitivity analysis of Taylor truncation (Fig. 8) that provides some insight into how truncation order affects Rayleigh quotient preservation.
weaknesses: The main theoretical result (Theorem 1) is essentially a trivial corollary of Wang et al. (2023): any norm-preserving map cannot change the norm of its input, so if the target norm varies on spheres, the approximation error is lower-bounded by that variance. It does not prove that unitary convolutions 'hurt performance' nor does it cover the proposed R-UniMesh model, which uses a non-unitary decoder.

The proposed encoder-decoder relaxation is simply a unitary encoder followed by a standard MLP/GCN decoder. There is no ablation isolating the benefit of the unitary encoder versus a decoder-only model of similar capacity, so the claimed advantage of the proposed relaxation is not convincingly established.
The GCN baseline fails to converge on all MeshPDE tasks (Table 2 dashes), making comparisons with that baseline uninformative and raising concerns about baseline tuning and fairness.

The mesh generalization relies on Assumption 1 (manifold, intrinsic Delaunay) and Robust Laplacian edge rewiring, but the paper does not state whether this preprocessing was applied or verified for the experimental meshes, so Corollary 1 may not hold in the reported experiments.

Missing comparison to the most relevant prior relaxation: Kiani et al. (2024) propose a relaxation for separable unitary convolutions, but the paper does not benchmark against it, leaving unclear whether the proposed relaxation is better.

Empirical claims are overstated. R-UniMesh is not best on wave or Cahn-Hilliard, and on WeatherBench2 it is not state-of-the-art and is often worse than baselines at longer lead times. The abstract's claim that the method 'outperforms several strong baselines' is only partially supported.

Reporting issues: Table 1 reports the best run out of 5, which can inflate results; Table 2 reports variance over test meshes/initializations but not over training runs; parameter counts are not compared across models despite claims about scaling.

The smoothness validation is limited: RE is a 1-hop mean metric, and the global 2-point correlation analysis in Sec. C.5 excludes R-UniMesh, so the claim that R-UniMesh best captures true smoothness beyond 1-hop is not tested.

Presentation and mathematical issues: the definition of SU(n) omits the unitarity condition; notation is inconsistent (L vs. \tilde{L}, A vs. \tilde{A}); there are typos such as 'seperable', 'Kroneckor', 'Multipliying', and 'discritizes'; and claims about being 'the first' to use cotangent weights in deep dynamics models may be overstated.

The core methodological novelty is modest: Taylor truncation is a natural truncation already considered by Kiani et al. for separable convolutions, and encoder-decoder is a standard hybrid architecture. The theoretical contribution is thin relative to its central role in the paper.

strengths: Provides a novel theoretical characterization (Theorem 1) of the approximation limits of unitary functions, showing the error is lower-bounded by the variance of the target's norm over SU(n) orbits. This gives a principled explanation for why unitary convolutions can be overconstrained for dynamics with angularly dependent norms, complementing the smoothness-preservation result of Kiani et al. (2024).

Introduces two concrete relaxation mechanisms for unitary convolutions (Taylor truncation and encoder-decoder), with a sensitivity analysis (Fig. 8) demonstrating that the KL divergence between input/output Rayleigh-quotient distributions decays exponentially with truncation order, supporting the claim that T_max=10 approximately preserves smoothness while smaller T_max relaxes it.

Generalizes the Rayleigh quotient and unitary convolution framework from graphs to meshes (Definition 3, Corollary 1), including a careful treatment of the Robust Laplacian and the intrinsic Delaunay criterion to ensure nonnegative weights so that the Rayleigh quotient remains a valid smoothness measure. The Kronecker-product proof of norm preservation and commutativity for the Lie mesh convolution is a reasonable technical contribution.

Empirical study is broad and multi-faceted: simulated PDEs (heat, wave, Cahn-Hilliard) on complex PyVista meshes plus real-world WeatherBench2 forecasting, with both accuracy (NRMSE/SMAPE/RMSE/ACC) and smoothness (Rayleigh error, 2-point correlation) metrics. The qualitative diagnostics (Fig. 1, Tab. 5) and per-timestep Rayleigh-quotient curves (Fig. 4) convincingly support the smoothness-matching claim on heat diffusion.
Reproducibility is reasonably addressed: code artifact, hyperparameters, model budgets, hardware, and explicit discussion of the small parameter budget and diverging runs.
weaknesses: The central theoretical claim is somewhat overstated. Theorem 1 only lower-bounds regression error by the orbit variance of ||f||; it does not by itself demonstrate that unitary convolutions 'hurt performance' relative to non-unitary models for general dynamics. The abstract's phrasing ('prove that unitary convolutions hurt performance for such tasks') is stronger than what is actually established, and the bound is not shown to be tight for the practical setting.

Technical carelessness in the theory section: SU(n) is defined as {U : det(U)=1}, omitting the unitarity condition U†U=I, which is incorrect. The proof of Corollary 1 also mixes notation (exp(AXW) vs exp(ÃXW), and 'symmetric edge weighting Ã = W ⊙ A') in ways that obscure which matrix the commutativity argument applies to.

The empirical picture is more mixed than the narrative suggests. R-UNIMESH is clearly best only on heat diffusion; on the wave equation it has the worst SMAPE among converged models (385.2 vs. EMAN 301.0), and on Cahn-Hilliard it is not the best on NRMSE or RE (EMAN/Transformer/Hermes are better on RE). The claim of broadly outperforming strong baselines is task-dependent.

Many baselines fail to converge (dashes throughout Tab. 2), and all models are constrained to a small ~40,000-50,000 parameter budget, which limits the strength and generality of the comparisons. The non-convergence of GCN and EGNN is not deeply analyzed.

The weather-forecasting contribution is weak: R-UNIMESH is below SOTA, uses a simplified latitude-longitude-derived mesh rather than a more standard icosahedral mesh, and the authors themselves note mesh optimization is left to future work. This reduces the significance of the real-world result.

The encoder-decoder 'relaxation' keeps the encoder fully unitary and only breaks unitarity in the decoder; it is arguably not a relaxation of the unitary convolution itself but rather an addition of an unconstrained head, which somewhat weakens the framing of the two relaxations as parallel alternatives.
